doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Louis Armstrong, Basie and New York studio scene
title: New York's studio and network staff bands, and the 300 who got the work
summary: Hinton explains New York made most American recordings, with network bands of 66 men; only about 300 of 37,000 union members got studio work and Black players were let in late.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well you know the whole…that period that you are describing was a unique period, both in the recording business and it was the embryo time of television. In those days they had staff bands at CBS and NBC and places like that.

Yeah 66 men there was. And it was…time is completely different now. But you see during those times we were making 75 percent of all the recording music made in America. It was made right here in New York City. It practically invented the TV jingle. The jingle was really an invention that came out of New York. Bob Howard and some of those guys were doing it on those local stations. So there was a lot of work. Then we had the three networks each using 66 musicians each and we still had all of the hotels in the world, more than anyplace else.

Yeah. So it was a couple of thousand musicians that were needed for gigs. So we had all of these things to work from and we had Local 82 then. We had 37,000 musicians in Local 82. And all of this work was done by like 300 musicians.
All of that studio work. So if you were lucky enough to get into that 300, you were pretty cool.

And it hadn‟t gotten to let any black guys in until the later half of the 40;s and the 50‟s because all the great song players were Benny Goodman, Charlie Margus, Vanny Kline and Bob Bitty Butterfield. Bitty Butterfield was seen as a more modern guy, helping out to do things. I remember Billy Hacket also, he was with the guys that kind of helped get some guys into the studios.
